chapter: Family band and learning to play
title: Teaching O'Bannon to play jazz by humming and scatting
summary: Tate explains to O'Bannon how to improvise by humming a solo; he played changes without knowing the theory.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I had a problem, like trying to teach him how to play jazz. So he says, "Well, what do you do?" He says, "How do you feel?" I says, "Well, look, Frank, the only thing," I says, "sometime I hum a solo in my mind," and I would take like "My Blue Heaven" and I would say like what we call now scat it." So I says, "I'll try to play as close to that as I possibly can." He said, "Oh, I get it." I says, "And get that in your mind." I says, "Just hum something in your mind," I says, "and you can write." I says, "Just write out something like in your mind, how you'd like to do it." So I hipped him to that, you know, and he said, "Well, I can't write -- I get kind of tied up on my time." But you know, I'd say in six months, man, he was taking some nice solos and things and I really felt like -- he told me, he says, "You
know --" I says, "Just hum, get a tune in your mind and that you think you'd want to play variations off of and do it," I says, "and that's the only way you --"
Then now I'm 13, I know I'm 13 then, 13.
So you weren't thinking in terms of chord changes?
I was doing it, but I didn't know what they were.
That phrase was not current among....
No, I didn't know what that was until -- and how to really form chord changes until I hired Earl Bostic myself in the first big band I ever worked with. I'll tell you about that.

So -- but now Malone had tried to tell me this, this other boy, but I couldn't get with that. I just didn't know -- he told me like C, E, G, C and all that kind of stuff. So he was telling me, says, "Now you got to --" He says, "You're doing it, but you don't know what you're doing with it." He says, "You don't know what key you're in, do you, half the time?" I says, "No, really." So he told me how to -- he says, "Well, whatever your last note ends on, that's just about the key it's on." He says, "Of course, there's major and there are minors and things." So when he went into that, he really lost me, you know what I mean? Because I was just
playing and I really didn't -- but I learned how to read.
